text: Mount drive motors inboard and belt-drive each mecanum wheel, so the wheel pods stay narrow and protected.
Single-stage 9t pinion to 108t gear gives 12:1 on bare 6000 rpm motors with no gearbox.
Mount drive motors in pairs on one plate per side, so each half of the drivetrain comes out as a module.
Steer coaxial swerve modules with Axon Mini servos on belts, so steering uses no motor ports.
Add polycarbonate outer plates over exposed drive gears to keep game pieces and fingers out.
Lay drive motors flat and turn them through miter gears into belts, freeing the space between the side plates.
Use a 6000 rpm motor directly on the intake for a fast pickup without a gearbox.
A servo-tilted ramp between intake and turret lets the robot hold balls or feed them on demand.
Turn a compliant wheel at each front corner through bevel gears so balls are pulled in from the sides too.
Intakes at the front and back on separate motors let the robot collect while driving either way.
Split the intake into a front compliant-wheel stage and a separately powered middle stage, so balls keep moving into storage.
Turn intake power 90° with a 2:1 bevel set so the motor lies along the side and the roller spans the full width.
Ten compliant wheels on one long shaft make a cheap full-width intake for 7 cm balls.
Add a separate flywheel mass on the shooter shaft so wheel speed drops less between shots.
Drive one flywheel shaft with two motors through 1:1 belts for faster spin-up and recovery.
Belt the counter roller off the flywheel shaft with double pulleys so their speeds stay locked together.
Power the flywheel and the counter roller from one motor through belts, saving a motor for other mechanisms.
Line the counter roller with surgical tubing so it grips the ball without a separate wheel.
Move the hood with a servo through a gear sector so the shot angle can change with distance.
Give each storage slot its own servo kicker so balls can be fired in any color order.
Laser distance sensors in storage count balls without depending on color.
Put color sensors at the ramp to count or sort pieces before the shooter.
Pair two color sensors per storage slot so artifact color reads reliably wherever the ball sits.
Put color sensors along the storage ramp so the robot knows the order of stored artifacts.
Surgical-tubing rollers along an inclined ramp carry balls from the intake up to the turret.
Turn the turret on a large ring gear (205T driven by 60T) for fine aiming resolution from a small actuator.
Build the turret frame from carbon-fiber tubes and printed mounts to keep weight off the turret bearing.
Route turret wires through a drag-chain ring (inner and outer wiring guides) so the turret turns without a slip ring.
Use a thin-section ring bearing (Kaydon KA060XP0) for the turret; it is flat and leaves the middle open for balls.
Mount the Limelight on the turret so the camera turns with the shooter and stays on the goal.
Gang three servos onto one turret ring gear for a fast, strong turret without using a motor port.
Drive the turret with two servos and read position from an absolute encoder instead of using a motor slot.
